1.text:
Where Does Carbon Go, and Where Does Our Energy Come From?

This is the last deck of Quarter 2, and it ties everything together. Earth works like one big machine whose parts trade carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus and water back and forth. And people take energy, stone, water and soil from those same systems.

Here's the big idea: every resource is part of a cycle. Coal is buried carbon. Groundwater is part of the water cycle. Soil is weathered rock plus life.

Along the way we'll visit our neighbors again. Venus shows what happens when Earth's carbon thermostat breaks, Mars shows a water cycle that shut down, and the Moon and asteroids show which space resources are real and which are still science fiction.

Did you know? Earth is 4.54 billion years old, and most of its carbon is stored not in the air or in living things, but in rocks.

2.text:
Today I Can...

Here's what you'll be able to do by the end of this deck. Copy these into your notebook as "I can" statements and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one.

I can describe Earth as four interacting spheres. I can trace carbon and oxygen through the fast and slow cycles. I can explain how rock weathering acts as a thermostat. I can diagram the nitrogen and phosphorus cycles and how people affect them. I can evaluate renewable vs nonrenewable resources. I can explain how Indiana's coal formed and why it's limited. I can analyze Indiana's electricity mix from EIA data. I can explain limestone, groundwater and soil as Indiana resources.

Three more are enrichment goals that are part of this course. I can compare Earth's thermostat with Venus's runaway greenhouse. I can explain how Mars lost its water cycle. And I can sort space resources into known and speculative.

3.text:
Earth Is Four Spheres in One

The Earth system is the geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere, all trading matter and energy. The geosphere (also called the lithosphere) is rock and land. The hydrosphere is water. The atmosphere is air. The biosphere is life.

These spheres aren't stacked like layers of a cake. They overlap and swap materials all the time. C, O, N, P and water cross every border. Rain dissolves rock. Plants pull CO2 from the air. Volcanoes add gas to the air. Oceans absorb CO2. Roots and worms build soil.

Keep these four spheres in mind. Every cycle in this deck moves stuff between them.

Did you know? NASA sometimes adds a fifth sphere, the cryosphere, for all of Earth's ice.

4.text:
Carbon Moves Fast & Slow

The carbon cycle is carbon moving among rock, ocean, air and life. Carbon travels on two loops at very different speeds.

The fast loop runs through life, over days to a lifetime. Air holds carbon as CO2 and CH4 (methane). Plants take in CO2 by photosynthesis and give off oxygen, while respiration and decay put CO2 back. The ocean also swaps CO2 with the air.

The slow loop runs through rock and takes 100 to 200 million years. Shells sink to the seafloor and become limestone, which holds the most carbon of all. Plant and animal remains buried in mud become shale and fossil fuels. Volcanoes return carbon to the air. But humans have added a shortcut: burning fuels takes carbon that's been locked up for millions of years and releases it in seconds.

Did you know? People release about 100 times or more CO2 each year than all volcanoes put together.

5.text:
Rocks Are Earth's Slow Thermostat

A thermostat keeps a house from getting too hot or too cold. Earth has one too, built out of rock. The weathering thermostat works like this: more CO2 warms Earth, rain dissolves more rock and pulls CO2 back out.

Follow the loop. More CO2 in air makes it warmer, with more rain. That means faster rock weathering, because carbonic acid rain dissolves rock. The dissolved ions wash to the sea, where creatures build them into shells. That carbon gets buried as limestone. CO2 drops, and Earth cools.

There's a catch: this thermostat takes a few hundred thousand years to work. It can't fix today's fast human CO2 increase on any human timescale.

Did you know? When the Himalaya rose up, starting 50 million years ago, the fresh rock pulled extra carbon out of the air and may have helped cool Earth. That's the leading hypothesis, but scientists still debate it.

6.text:
Venus: The Thermostat Failed

Venus's surface is 464 °C, under 92 bar of air. What went wrong? On Earth, the ocean and limestone keep carbon locked in rock, so our air is just 1 bar, mostly N2.

On Venus, the carbon is in the air: 96.5% CO2, no oceans. Venus may have had oceans long ago. But extra heat evaporated the water and released gas from rocks, which trapped more heat, in a runaway greenhouse.

Some scientists think Venus may always have been dry. If it did have oceans, once they were gone there was no more rain to dissolve rock and pull CO2 back down. The thermostat from Slide 5 stopped working. That's the leading explanation, though scientists are still working out exactly what started Venus down this path.

Did you know? Earth isn't about to become Venus. The Sun is slowly getting brighter, but models say Earth's oceans won't boil away for at least about a billion years.

8.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Think about the slow loop from Slides 4 and 5. Most of Earth's carbon is stored in...

A) rocks, B) the air, C) the ocean, or D) forests? Choose your answer and explain why. Don't just picture the fast cycle!

9.text:
Nitrogen Needs Bacteria

Air is 78% N2, nitrogen gas. Every living thing needs nitrogen to make proteins and DNA. But here's the problem: plants can't use N2 straight from the air, because its atoms are locked together by a very strong triple bond.

Enter bacteria. Nitrogen fixation is when bacteria turn N2 gas from the air into forms plants can use. Some of these fixing bacteria live in root nodules, little bumps on the roots of plants like peas and beans.

Then more bacteria take over. Waste and decay release ammonium, NH4+, in ammonification. Next, in nitrification, other bacteria turn it into nitrite, NO2-, and then nitrate, NO3-. Plants take up NO3-. Finally, denitrification turns nitrate back into N2 gas, completing the loop. People add extra nitrogen with fertilizer.

Did you know? Nitrogen gas is harmless. The problem is too much fixed nitrogen washing into water.

10.text:
Phosphorus Has No Gas Stage

The phosphorus cycle is phosphate moving from rock to soil, life and water, never through the air. That makes it different from carbon and nitrogen. Phosphorus is in your DNA, and in your bones.

Follow the loop. Weathering of uplifted rock releases PO43-, phosphate, in soil. Runoff carries it to algae and animals, and into lakes and the ocean. When those living things die, their remains settle as ocean sediment, which slowly becomes new rock. It only comes back to land by uplift over millions of years.

People speed things up with fertilizer and sewage. They send extra P to water, where it feeds algae. In lakes and rivers, phosphorus is often the nutrient in shortest supply, so a little extra makes algae grow like crazy.

11.text:
Farm Runoff Makes a Dead Zone

In July 2025, the Gulf dead zone measured 4,402 sq mi. For comparison, the 5-year average was larger, and the 2035 goal is much smaller. The bar graph shows how many sq mi of low-oxygen bottom water there are.

How does a farm make a dead zone hundreds of miles away? Fertilizer and manure on fields wash into a river as N and P runoff. Down at the Gulf, those nutrients feed a giant algae bloom. Then the dead algae sink and decay, and the decay uses up the oxygen. Bottom water drops to 2 mg/L oxygen or less, too low for many fish and bottom animals.

Did you know? The five-year average is still more than twice the goal of under 1,900 square miles by 2035.

12.text:
Mars Lost Its Water Cycle

A water cycle needs liquid water and an atmosphere thick enough to hold on to it. Mars once had both. Back then, an ocean covered the north, about 19% of the surface.

Over billions of years, Mars dried out. Light H escaped to space after UV light split water molecules. Scientists estimate about 87% of early Mars's water was lost to space.

Now Mars is dry, with ice at the poles. Its air is only 6.36 mb, mostly CO2, so liquid water can't last at the surface. That's why scientists call Mars a "runaway refrigerator," the opposite of Venus.

Did you know? The 87% figure is a model estimate based on heavy water in Mars's air, not a direct measurement.

15.text:
Renewable or Nonrenewable?

A nonrenewable resource forms far more slowly than people use it, like coal, oil and gas. These are finite: they take millions of years to form. Once we use them up, they're gone.

Renewable resources are naturally replenished: solar, wind, hydropower, biomass and geothermal. But "renewable" doesn't mean unlimited. The wind doesn't always blow, and the Sun sets every night.

Indiana has learned this lesson before. In the Trenton Field gas boom of 1886 to 1913, people drilled so wastefully that the gas ran out fast.

Did you know? Fossil fuels don't come from dinosaurs. Coal comes from ancient plants, and oil formed from tiny ocean life.

16.text:
Indiana's Coal Was a Swamp Forest

Coal is carbon-rich rock made from buried swamp plants, squeezed and heated. You met this story in Deck 10. Step 1: a swamp forest grows. Step 2: it's buried under mud and sand. Step 3: heat and pressure turn it into coal.

Indiana's coal formed in the Pennsylvanian period, 323 to 299 million years ago. It's all bituminous coal, found in SW Indiana, including Knox County.

In carbon-cycle terms, coal is carbon that plants pulled from the air long ago and locked into the slow loop. Burning it sends that carbon back to the air in seconds.

Did you know? Indiana has about 57 billion tons of unmined coal, but only about 17 billion tons can be dug up with today's technology.

17.text:
Indiana Still Runs on Coal & Gas

In 2024, 41.8% of Indiana's in-state electricity generation came from coal (EIA). That's down a lot. Look at the bars: in 2000, coal was 95%.

By 2024 the mix had changed. Coal was 41.8%, natural gas 41.1%, wind 10.6% and solar 3.2%, with a little "other." In about 20 years, Indiana shifted from nearly all coal toward gas, wind and solar.

Still, coal and gas together supply more than 80% of Indiana's power. Natural gas burns cleaner than coal, but it's still a nonrenewable fossil fuel.

Did you know? You might see 38.3% for coal somewhere else. That number counts only utility-owned plants, while 41.8% counts all of them. Always check what's being counted.

18.text:
Evaluate Indiana's Power Mix

Time to work with real data from the US EIA, Indiana State Electricity Profile, Table 5. Here are the percentages. 2000: coal 95, natural gas 1.6, wind 0, solar 0. 2010: coal 89.7, gas 5.2, wind 2.3, solar 0. 2020: coal 53, gas 35.6, wind 7, solar 0.4. 2024: coal 41.8, gas 41.1, wind 10.6, solar 3.2.

Fill in the "fossil total %" (coal plus gas) and "wind + solar %" columns for each year. Note that the rows won't add up to 100%, because small sources are left out.

Then graph the trend and argue: what should Indiana build next? Back up your argument with evidence.

19.text:
Indiana Built America's Cities

Up to 75% of the limestone in North American buildings came from one small Indiana belt (IGWS). The belt is only about 10 by 30 mi.

This is the Salem Limestone, about 340 million years old, made from shells in an ancient sea. It's pure, thick and easy to carve, which made it famous. It built the Empire State Building, among many others.

Indiana's stone isn't just for fancy buildings. Crushed stone and gravel are mined statewide for roads and concrete. Limestone is nonrenewable on a human timescale, but the supply is large.

Did you know? Indiana limestone was first quarried in 1827, in Monroe County.

20.text:
Groundwater Fills Rock Like a Sponge

An aquifer is saturated rock or sediment below the water table that can supply a well. Groundwater doesn't usually sit in underground lakes. It fills tiny spaces between grains, like water in a sponge.

Look at the diagram. Rain soaks in. The top of the soaked zone is the water table. Below it, a sand and gravel aquifer holds water. A clay layer can seal water below it into a confined aquifer. Wells and streams connect to it. Pumping lowers the water table, which can dry up wells and streams.

In north Indiana, aquifers are glacial sand and gravel. In south Indiana, where the bedrock holds little water, people rely on reservoirs like Monroe Lake.

Did you know? About two-thirds of Hoosiers depend on groundwater for their drinking water.

21.text:
Indiana Soil Started as Glacial Till

Soil is weathered rock plus living and dead matter, built up over time. It isn't just dirt. Look at the layers: topsoil on top, then subsoil, then parent material: till left by the glaciers. Worms and roots mix it all together.

What makes soil? Scientists list five soil-forming factors: climate, organisms, relief (the shape of the land), parent material and time.

Indiana's official state soil is the Miami soil. It formed in glacial till dropped 15,000 to 22,000 years ago. That means it took thousands of years to build, so soil is renewable only very slowly.

Did you know? Indiana has 555 named kinds of soil.

22.text:
Model: Soil & Groundwater

For Part B, a cup aquifer: build layers of gravel, sand and clay. Mark the water table. Pump a well, feed a stream, and add one human effect, like paving or pollution.

23.text:
Space Resources: Real or Not Yet?

Earth's resources are limited, so people dream about mining space. Let's sort the claims by evidence. Moon polar ice: CONFIRMED. Scientists have found ice in crater shadows near the Moon's poles. Someday it might supply water, air and rocket fuel for explorers. None has been mined yet.

Helium-3 for fusion: SPECULATIVE. Moon soil contains 3He, but only at parts per billion, and fusion reactors that run on it don't exist yet.

Asteroid mining: SPECULATIVE. NASA's mission to asteroid Bennu brought back 121.6 g, the entire Bennu sample. So far, we have only grams of samples, not tons.

Did you know? Indiana produces more than 80 million tons of sand, gravel and crushed stone a year. Compare that to 121.6 grams from Bennu!

25.text:
Exit Ticket

You traced Earth's cycles and resources today. Show what you've learned with three questions.

First, how does rain on rock keep Earth from turning into Venus? Second, how can fertilizer on a farm make a dead zone far away? Third, pick one Indiana resource. Is it renewable or not? Give one number and its source.

When you're done, look back at your "I can" list from Slide 2 and rate yourself again.

26.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask you to do, in plain words.

ES.3.1: make flowcharts of how carbon and oxygen move between rock, water, life and air, including CO2 and methane, and explain how farming, industry, ocean temperature and volcanoes speed up or slow down that cycling. ES.3.2: diagram the nitrogen cycle through all four spheres, the phosphorus cycle without the air, and explain how people change both. ES.3.4: compare sustainable and nonrenewable resources, explain what happens when we overuse limited resources, and weigh the benefits of developing sustainable ones.

ES.4.3: show the water cycle locally and globally, including how groundwater and surface water connect and how people affect water. ES.5.3: model the steps from weathering to erosion, transport, deposition, and new soil and sedimentary rock, and tell physical from chemical weathering.
